segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Six days later Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he was transformed before them: his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as the light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Peter spoke up and said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here—one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was still speaking, suddenly a bright cloud overshadowed them, and there came a voice from the cloud, saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “This is my Son, the beloved, with whom I am well pleased. Listen to him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were greatly afraid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus came and touched them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up, and do not be afraid.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus himself, alone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the disciples asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Elijah is indeed coming, and he will restore all things.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him but did to him whatever they wanted. In the same way the Son of Man also is about to suffer at their hands.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to the crowd, a man approached him, knelt before him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and suffers terribly; he often falls into the fire and often into the water.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “O faithless and twisted generation, how long will I be with you? How long will I put up with you? Bring him here to me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed from that hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples came to Jesus by themselves and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why could we not cast it out?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Because of your little faith. For truly I tell you, if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and they will kill him, and on the third day he will be raised.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were greatly distressed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax approached Peter and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Does your teacher not pay the two-drachma tax?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when Peter came into the house, Jesus spoke first and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or poll tax—from their sons or from others?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “From others,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Then the sons are free.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that we do not give them offense, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth you will find a four-drachma coin. Take that and give it to them for me and for you.”

notes.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for a change of form or appearance, and it is the same verb rendered “transformed” in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18. “Transfigured” comes from the Latin translation and survives in English almost only as a name for this event. Nearly all English versions keep “transfigured” here; the plain word is used so that the reader hears what a Greek reader heard and can see the link with Paul’s usage.

The Greek word is the everyday one for a tent or hut. The Greek Old Testament uses it both for Israel’s wilderness sanctuary and for the huts of the Feast of Booths, and either association may lie behind Peter’s offer. Older versions have “tabernacles”; modern versions divide between “tents”, “shelters” and “dwellings”.

The expectation comes from Malachi 4:5–6, where God promises to send Elijah before the day of the Lord to turn the hearts of fathers and children back to one another. The Greek Old Testament uses this same verb, “restore”, in that passage. Jesus affirms the expectation and then, in the next verse, says it has already been fulfilled in John the Baptist.

notes.traditional: is a lunatic; is an epileptic
notes.note: The Greek verb literally means to be affected by the moon, reflecting the ancient belief that the moon’s phases brought on such attacks. The symptoms described, sudden falls into fire and water, are those of a seizure disorder, and many modern versions say “epileptic”. “Has seizures” describes the condition without importing either the ancient theory or a modern diagnosis; verse 18 attributes the boy’s affliction to a demon.

The wording echoes the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:5 and 32:20, where Israel in the wilderness is called a crooked and twisted generation in whom there is no faithfulness. It is not clear whether Jesus is addressing the disciples, the crowd, or his contemporaries as a whole. The Greek word rendered “faithless” is the negative of the word for faith that appears in verse 20.

The Greek says only “rebuked him” or “rebuked it”, and then “the demon came out of him”. The pronoun could refer to the boy or to the demon, since the form is the same for both. Most translators and commentators take it as the demon, as here, in line with the parallel accounts in Mark and Luke.

notes.phrase: nothing will be impossible for you
notes.note: Many later manuscripts continue with a verse 21: “But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting.” It is absent from important early manuscripts and is widely judged to have been added from the parallel in Mark 9:29, so the Greek text followed here omits it and the numbering passes from 20 to 22. In the same verse, many manuscripts read “unbelief” where the text followed here has “little faith”.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody or power. The Gospels use it for what Judas, the chief priests and Pilate each do to Jesus in turn, and one English rendering lets that chain be seen. Most versions have “delivered” or “betrayed” here; the lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense, and many scholars regard “betray” as an inference from context, though others defend it where Judas is the subject.

The Greek plays on one word: the “Son of Man” is to be handed over into the hands of “men”, meaning human beings generally. “Human hands” keeps the generic sense while leaving an echo of the wordplay.

The Greek simply says “the two-drachma pieces”. This was the yearly contribution of half a shekel that adult Jewish men paid for the upkeep of the Jerusalem temple, based on Exodus 30:13. Two drachmas was roughly two days’ wages for a laborer. It was a religious levy, not a Roman tax.

“Sons” may mean the kings’ own children and household, who are exempt from what the kings levy, or more broadly their own people as opposed to subject foreigners. The first is the more common reading and gives the sharper point: since the tax is for God’s house, God’s children are free of it. On either reading Jesus claims exemption and pays anyway.

notes.traditional: a piece of money; a shekel
notes.note: The Greek names the coin, a stater, which was worth four drachmas. That is exactly the two-drachma tax for two people, which is why Jesus says it will cover “me and you”.
